title: Orphic Color: “Sonia Delaunay”—Prelude and Fugue No.11, Book II
content_blocks: These were inspired by paintings by the Ukrainian-born French artist Sonia Delaunay: Philomène (1907), a Fauvist portrait of a seemingly-still woman, and Electric Prisms (1914), what she and her husband, painter Robert Delaunay, termed an “Orphic” depiction of the glow from newly-installed electric lamplights. Both burst with energy—which she described as “an extreme exaltation of color with complete flatness.”

In the prelude, a recurring quite-simple chord progression belies the energy of the inherently-modulatory “HyperLydian” mode, created for this pair of pieces.  That same mode is used in the constantly-refracting and colorful fugue, in which a short and narrow-ranged subject nevertheless contains boundless energy that bursts forth over the course of the piece.

The piano preparation for this pair of pieces involves spreading a blanket or large, heavy towels over the center of the piano. This both gives the sound a hushed and beautiful quality, appropriate to Philomène, especially, but also is an homage to Delaunay’s most important medium, which was fabric and quilting.

David Kaplan’s enthusiasm for these pieces was not dampened by the towels. You can see his delightful performances without video of the of the Prelude and Fugue and with video of the Prelude and Fugue.
“An extreme exaltation of color with complete flatness”— hushed by blankets or towels.
